title: The Golden Bird
paragraphs: A certain king had a beautiful garden, and in the garden grew a tree that bore golden apples. The apples were counted regularly, and just as they were starting to ripen, the king found that one went missing every night. This made him very angry, and he ordered the gardener to watch under the tree all night long. The gardener sent his eldest son to keep watch, but around midnight the young man fell asleep, and by morning another apple was gone. Next the second son was told to watch, and at midnight he fell asleep too, and in the morning another apple had vanished. Then the third son offered to take a turn. At first the gardener refused, afraid some harm might come to him, but in the end he gave in, and the young man lay down under the tree to watch. As the clock struck twelve, he heard a rustling in the air, and a bird of pure gold came flying in. While it was snapping at one of the apples with its beak, the gardener’s son jumped up and shot an arrow at it. The arrow did the bird no harm, though it shook loose a golden feather from its tail before it flew away. In the morning the golden feather was brought to the king, and the whole council was summoned. They all agreed it was worth more than everything the kingdom owned. But the king said, “One feather is no use to me. I must have the whole bird.”

So the gardener’s eldest son set off, sure he would find the golden bird easily. After he had gone a short way, he came to a wood, and at the edge of it he saw a fox sitting. He took up his bow and got ready to shoot. But the fox said, “Don’t shoot me, and I’ll give you good advice. I know what you’re after: you want to find the golden bird. This evening you will reach a village, and there you will see two inns facing each other. One of them is bright and lovely to look at. Don’t go in there. Spend the night in the other, however poor and shabby it seems.” But the son thought, “What could an animal like this know about it?” So he shot his arrow at the fox and missed, and the fox lifted its tail over its back and ran into the wood. The young man went on his way and in the evening reached the village with the two inns. In one of them people were singing, dancing and feasting. The other looked dirty and poor. “I’d be a fool,” he said, “to go into that rundown place and pass up this charming one.” So he went into the grand inn, ate and drank as much as he pleased, and forgot the bird and his own country too.

Time went by, and since the eldest son did not come home and no word of him arrived, the second son set out, and the same thing happened to him. He met the fox, who gave him the same good advice. But when he came to the two inns, his eldest brother was standing at the window of the one where the merrymaking was, and he called to him to come in. The second son could not resist the temptation. He went in, and just like his brother he forgot the golden bird and his country.

More time went by, and now the youngest son wanted to go out into the wide world to look for the golden bird. For a long while his father would not hear of it. He was very fond of this son, and feared that some misfortune would befall him too and keep him from coming back. But the young man would not settle at home, and in the end it was agreed that he could go. When he reached the wood, he met the fox and heard the same good advice. This son was grateful to the fox and did not try to kill it, as his brothers had done. So the fox said, “Sit on my tail, and you’ll travel faster.” He sat down, the fox began to run, and off they went over stock and stone so fast that their hair whistled in the wind.

When they reached the village, the son followed the fox’s advice. Without even looking around, he went to the shabby inn and rested there all night in comfort. In the morning the fox came again and met him as he was setting out. “Go straight ahead,” it said, “until you come to a castle. In front of it a whole troop of soldiers lie fast asleep, snoring. Pay no attention to them. Go into the castle and keep walking until you come to a room where the golden bird sits in a wooden cage. Beside it stands a beautiful golden cage, but don’t try to take the bird out of the plain cage and put it in the fine one, or you’ll be sorry.” Then the fox stretched out its tail again, the young man sat down, and off they went over stock and stone until their hair whistled in the wind.

In front of the castle gate everything was just as the fox had said. The son went in and found the chamber where the golden bird hung in a wooden cage, with the golden cage standing below it, and the three golden apples that had been lost lying close by. Then he thought, “It would be absurd to carry off such a fine bird in this shabby cage.” So he opened the door, took hold of the bird and put it into the golden cage. But the bird let out such a loud scream that all the soldiers woke up. They seized him and carried him before the king. The next morning the court met to judge him, and when everything had been heard, it sentenced him to death, unless he brought the king the golden horse that could run as swiftly as the wind. If he did that, he would be given the golden bird as his own.

So he set out on his journey once more, sighing, in deep despair, when suddenly his friend the fox met him and said, “You see now what has happened because you didn’t listen to my advice. Still, I will tell you how to find the golden horse, if you’ll do as I say. Go straight on until you come to the castle where the horse stands in his stall. The groom will be lying beside him, fast asleep and snoring. Lead the horse away quietly, but be sure to put the old leather saddle on him, and not the golden one that hangs close by.” Then the son sat down on the fox’s tail, and off they went over stock and stone until their hair whistled in the wind.

Everything went well, and the groom lay snoring with his hand on the golden saddle. But when the son looked at the horse, he thought it a great pity to put the leather saddle on it. “I’ll give him the good one,” he said. “I’m sure he deserves it.” As he picked up the golden saddle, the groom woke and shouted so loudly that all the guards ran in and took him prisoner. In the morning he was brought before the court again and sentenced to die. But it was agreed that if he could bring the beautiful princess to them, he would live and be given the bird and the horse as his own.

He went on his way, very sorrowful. But the old fox came to him and said, “Why didn’t you listen to me? If you had, you would have carried off both the bird and the horse. Still, I will give you advice once more. Go straight on, and in the evening you will arrive at a castle. At twelve o’clock at night the princess goes to the bathing-house. Walk up to her and give her a kiss, and she will let you lead her away. But make sure you don’t let her go and say goodbye to her father and mother.” Then the fox stretched out its tail, and off they went over stock and stone until their hair whistled again.

When they reached the castle, everything was as the fox had said. At twelve o’clock the young man met the princess on her way to the bath and kissed her, and she agreed to run away with him. But she begged him, with many tears, to let her say goodbye to her father. At first he refused, but she wept harder and harder and fell at his feet, until at last he gave in. The moment she entered her father’s house, however, the guards woke up, and he was taken prisoner again.

He was brought before the king, who said, “You will never have my daughter unless you dig away, within eight days, the hill that blocks the view from my window.” This hill was so huge that the whole world could not have carried it off. After he had worked for seven days and done very little, the fox came and said, “Lie down and go to sleep. I’ll do the work for you.” In the morning he woke and the hill was gone. He went cheerfully to the king and told him that, now the hill was removed, he must give him the princess.

The king had to keep his word, so the young man and the princess went off together. Then the fox came and said to him, “We’ll have all three: the princess, the horse and the bird.” “Ah,” said the young man, “that would be wonderful, but how can you manage it?”

“If you will only listen,” said the fox, “it can be done. When you come to the king and he asks for the beautiful princess, you must say, ‘Here she is!’ He will be overjoyed. Then you will mount the golden horse they are to give you and reach out your hand to say farewell, but shake hands with the princess last. Then swiftly lift her onto the horse behind you, dig your spurs into his sides, and gallop away as fast as you can.”

All went well. Then the fox said, “When you come to the castle where the bird is, I’ll stay at the door with the princess, and you will ride in and speak to the king. When he sees that it is the right horse, he will bring out the bird. But you must sit still and say you want to look at it, to see whether it is the true golden bird. And when you have it in your hand, ride away.”

This too happened as the fox had said. They carried off the bird, the princess mounted again, and they rode on to a great wood. Then the fox came and said, “Please kill me, and cut off my head and my feet.” But the young man refused to do it. So the fox said, “Then I will at least give you some good advice. Beware of two things: don’t ransom anyone from the gallows, and don’t sit down beside any river.” Then it went away. “Well,” thought the young man, “it’s no hard matter to follow that advice.”

He rode on with the princess until at last he came to the village where he had left his two brothers. There he heard a great noise and uproar, and when he asked what the matter was, the people said, “Two men are about to be hanged.” As he came nearer, he saw that the two men were his brothers, who had turned robbers. So he said, “Is there no way to save them?” But the people said no, unless he were willing to hand over all his money to the scoundrels and buy their freedom. He did not stop to think it over. He paid what was asked, his brothers were released, and they went on with him toward home.

When they came to the wood where the fox had first met them, it was so cool and pleasant that the two brothers said, “Let’s sit down by the river and rest a while, and eat and drink.” He said yes, forgot the fox’s warning, and sat down by the river. While he suspected nothing, they came up behind him, threw him down the bank, took the princess, the horse and the bird, and went home to the king their master. “We won all this by our own efforts,” they said. There was great rejoicing, but the horse would not eat, the bird would not sing, and the princess wept.

The youngest son fell to the bottom of the riverbed. Luckily it was nearly dry, but his bones were almost broken, and the bank was so steep that he could find no way out. Then the old fox came once more and scolded him for not following its advice, since otherwise no harm would have come to him. “Still,” it said, “I can’t leave you here. Grab hold of my tail and hang on tight.” Then it pulled him out of the river, and as he climbed onto the bank, it said to him, “Your brothers have set guards to kill you if they find you in the kingdom.” So he dressed himself as a poor man and came secretly to the king’s court. He had hardly stepped through the doors when the horse began to eat, the bird began to sing, and the princess stopped weeping. Then he went to the king and told him all about his brothers’ treachery. They were seized and punished, and he was given the princess again; and after the king’s death he inherited the kingdom.

A long while later, he went walking one day in the wood, and the old fox met him and begged him with tears in its eyes to kill it and cut off its head and feet. At last he did so, and in an instant the fox was changed into a man. He turned out to be the brother of the princess, who had been lost for many, many years.
